title: Association between traffic-related black carbon exposure and lung function among urban women.
ehr_evidence: Women were voluntary participants in the Maternal–Infant Smoking Study of East Boston, a prospective cohort originally designed to study the effects of pre- and postnatal tobacco smoke exposure on childhood lung growth and development and respiratory health.
summary: Prospective cohort study examining the association between long-term traffic-related black carbon exposure and lung function among urban women in Boston.
key_findings: BC per IQR increase was associated with a 1.1% decrease in FEV1 (95% CI, –2.5 to 0.3%), a 0.6% decrease in FVC (95% CI, –1.9 to 0.6%), and a 3.0% decrease in FEF25-75% (95% CI, –5.8 to –0.2%).
Former smokers experienced significant reductions in FEV1 (–4.4%), FVC (–3.1%), and FEF25-75% (–8.9%), while current smokers showed no significant effects.
Summer IQR increase in BC was associated with a –1.32% decrease in FEV1 (95% CI, –2.8 to 0.2%), –0.70% in FVC (95% CI, –2.1 to 0.2%), and –3.34% in FEF25-75% (95% CI, –6.3 to –0.4%).
population: 272 urban women aged 18-42 years recruited from an East Boston community health center during pregnancy
limitations: significant sample attrition over longitudinal follow-up
potential unmeasured or residual confounding, particularly regarding socioeconomic status
restricted variability in individual-level SES due to single-site recruitment
potential exposure misclassification from unmeasured work and other locations
use of predicted rather than observed exposure measurements introducing Berkson-type measurement error
lack of data on other spatially variable pollutants like NO2 and ozone
